scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origins of Seungmu are uncertain, with little extant evidence.
Some theories link it to the monk Wonhyo or to the mocking of upper-class priests.
Once prohibited during the Joseon dynasty, it was transformed into a folk dance by kisaengs and later refashioned into stage art by Han Sŏngjun in 1936.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Seungmu is a form of art that communicates to the public.
It symbolizes the birth of the universe, the four azimuths, the course of life, and human emotions like joy, wrath, and sorrow.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed solo.
It begins with the dancer crouched on the ground, slowly expanding their motion.
The dancer uses long, white sleeves to create expressive shapes in the air.
Watch for Sleeve expansion.

Formation: Solo performance; utilizes space to represent the four azimuths.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by eight rhythmic cycles: yeombul, dodeuri, taryeong, jajin taryeong, gutgeori, dwit gutgeori, gujeong nori, and saesanjo.
The 'bubgo' (drum) is the most important instrument, serving as a central element of the performance.
Listen for the bubgo (drum).
The music is characterized by a progression of rhythmic cycles that shift from heavy, slow beats to faster, more sophisticated patterns, centered around the sound of the bubgo drum.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Lee Mae Bang (deceased 2015), Kim Myo Seon, Kim Myung Ja, and Han Young-suk are noted as masters or master assistants of this tradition.
The dance was improvised in variegated forms in different regions until the 1930s when various styles were archived and choreographed.
The dance is a descendant of folk art traditions and shares commonalities with Buddhist ritual dances, though it is distinct from them.
